summary: Source-specific routing, also called Source Address Dependent Routing, forwards packets according to both destination and source address instead of destination alone. This document describes an extension to the Babel routing protocol to support it.

plainLanguage.summary: Usually a router asks only where a packet is going. This document lets the Babel router also ask where it came from, and pick a road for each case.

questions: what is the babel source prefix sub-tlv
subtitle: How Babel routers can pick a path using the packet's source address as well as its destination.

tldr.problem: Ordinary next-hop routing looks only at the destination address, so a network with several providers cannot send each packet to the edge router that matches the provider its source address came from.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds a source prefix to Babel's tables and to the Update, Route Request and Seqno Request messages, carried in a mandatory Source Prefix sub-TLV (type 128). All routers use destination-first ordering to pick among matching routes.
tldr.outcome: Edge routers can announce default routes specific to the prefix of their provider, which makes multihoming with multiple addresses work without changes to hosts. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9079 is a Proposed Standard from August 2021. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The Homenet profile in RFC 9080 requires it for IPv6.

sections.title: Routing on More Than the Destination
sections.content:
The Babel routing protocol (RFC 8966) is a distance vector protocol for next-hop routing. Each node keeps a forwarding table of destination prefixes and next hops, and a packet follows the entry with the most specific prefix that contains its destination address.

That has two limits. A router A can only select a route ABC...Z if its neighbour B has selected BC...Z, and two packets with the same destination always follow the same route. Source-specific routing, also called Source Address Dependent Routing (SADR), lets the forwarding decision depend on the source address as well, so two packets with the same destination but different sources can take different paths.

This RFC describes the extension for Babel. It adds a source prefix to the data structures and to three TLVs, encoded with a mandatory sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: A router usually looks only at where a packet is going. This extension lets it also look at where the packet came from, and choose the road using both.

sections.title: Why It Is Needed: Multihoming and Other Uses
sections.content:
The main use is multihoming with multiple addresses. Classical multihoming needs a provider-independent address range announced to all providers, which is too costly for small networks. With ordinary provider-dependent addresses, a packet whose source address was allocated by provider A must leave through the edge router connected to A. If it leaves through B, it will most likely be filtered (dropped), in accordance with BCP 84.

So every host gets one address per provider, and the network must route each packet towards the router of the provider that matches its source address. Every edge router announces into the routing domain a default route specific to the prefix of its provider. The route propagates to the routers on the access link, and hosts simply send packets to their default router, with no network-layer host changes.

The RFC names two more uses. With tunnels and VPNs, a default route specific to the tunnel's prefix keeps the encapsulated packets (whose source is outside that prefix) from being routed back into the tunnel. With controlled anycast, each member of an anycast group can announce a route specific to its own client population, which the RFC calls simpler and more robust than manually tweaking metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a house with two mail carriers, each only accepting letters stamped with their own stamp. The sorter has to look at the stamp to hand each letter to the right carrier.

sections.title: Ordering Pairs of Prefixes
sections.content:
Plain routing relies on the "longest prefix rule", which works because any two prefixes are either disjoint or one is more specific than the other. Pairs of (destination, source) prefixes do not have that property. The RFC's example is (2001:db8:0:1::/64, ::/0) and (::/0, 2001:db8:0:2::/64): a packet can match both, and neither is more specific.

A finer ordering is needed, and every router in the domain must use the same one or persistent routing loops can occur. The RFC shows a chain A, B, C, D where B uses destination-first and C uses source-first ordering, so a matching packet bounces between B and C forever.

The document mandates destination-first ordering: entry R1 is preferred to R2 when R1's destination prefix is more specific, or the destination prefixes are equal and R1's source prefix is more specific. It argues this is more useful: a packet for a destination in an internal network should go there, not out towards the Internet because of a source-specific default route.
sections.plainLanguage: When two rules both fit a letter, everybody has to agree which rule wins first. Here they all agree to look at the destination first and the sender second.

sections.title: Tables and Forwarding
sections.content:
Three of Babel's conceptual tables gain a source prefix (sprefix, splen): the source table, the route table and the table of pending seqno requests. Each is now indexed by 5-tuples, for example (prefix, plen, sprefix, splen, router-id) for the source table. Data from the original protocol is stored with a zero-length source prefix, which matches exactly the same packets as before.

For forwarding, an implementation MUST use destination-first ordering. In practice that depends on the lower layers:

  • If they implement destination-first ordering, Babel SHOULD use them directly.
  • If they can hold source-specific routes but with the wrong semantics, Babel MUST either silently ignore source-specific routes or disambiguate the table with a suitable algorithm.
  • If they cannot hold source-specific routes, Babel MUST silently ignore them.
sections.plainLanguage: The router's notebooks get an extra column for the sender. If the machine that actually moves packets cannot use that column properly, the router just ignores those entries.

sections.title: Protocol Operation and Wildcards
sections.content:
Operation is unchanged apart from the source prefix. The Update, Route Request and Seqno Request TLVs may carry a Source Prefix sub-TLV. Because the sub-TLV is mandatory, an unextended node silently ignores the whole enclosing TLV. A node MUST NOT send a TLV with a zero-length source prefix; it sends no sub-TLV instead, and an extended node reads a TLV without the sub-TLV as having a zero-length source prefix.

On receiving a source-specific update, a node follows RFC 8966 as usual, except that the entry is indexed by (prefix, plen, sprefix, splen, neigh). Source-specific requests apply to the route table entry with the indicated source prefix.

Wildcard messages (address encoding 0) apply to all routes whatever their source prefix. A wildcard retraction applies to all routes learned from the sender, and a wildcard route request SHOULD get a full table dump including source-specific routes. A node MUST NOT send a wildcard retraction or wildcard request that carries a source prefix, and a receiver MUST ignore one that does.
sections.plainLanguage: The router adds a small sticker to its messages saying which senders the route is for. Old routers do not understand the sticker, so they skip the whole message.

sections.title: The Source Prefix Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The sub-TLV has type 128, a Length, a Source Plen and the Source Prefix. Source Plen is the prefix length in bits and MUST NOT be 0. The prefix takes Source Plen divided by 8 octets, rounded upwards, so the body is normally 1 plus that many octets.

If Length is smaller than that, the sub-TLV is corrupt and the whole enclosing TLV is ignored. If it is larger, the extra octets are silently ignored. A TLV with address encoding 0 that contains a Source Prefix sub-TLV, or one with more than one such sub-TLV, MUST be ignored entirely.

Babel compresses destination prefixes in Updates statefully, but the source prefix is never compressed. Destination prefixes in source-specific updates may still be compressed, and unextended implementations still update their parser state correctly while ignoring the TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small labelled box inside a message that holds the sender range. The label number is 128, and the box says how many bits of the range matter.

sections.title: Compatibility with Plain Babel
sections.content:
Mixing source-specific and non-source-specific routers in one domain preserves Babel's loop avoidance, so no persistent routing loops occur. The extension relies on mandatory sub-TLVs introduced in RFC 8966, so it is not compatible with the older Babel of RFC 6126. It MUST NOT be used in a domain where some routers implement RFC 6126, or persistent routing loops may occur.

The catch is starvation: plain routers discard source-specific routes, so unless enough non-source-specific routes exist they drop packets for destinations announced only by source-specific routers. When all source-specific routes come from a small set of edge routers, a sufficient fix is a connected source-specific backbone including all the edge routers, plus a non-source-specific default route towards that backbone.
sections.plainLanguage: New and old routers can share a network, but the old ones cannot see the special routes. To avoid leaving them stranded, give them one plain road that leads to the new routers.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The extension adds a sub-TLV and does not change Babel's own security properties. But the added flexibility may break administrators' assumptions. Route filtering written without source-specific routing in mind might be bypassed by a source-specific route. An administrator who assumes nothing is more specific than a host route, and uses one to steer traffic through a firewall, may find that a source-specific route can bypass the device in some topologies.

IANA allocated sub-TLV number 128 for the Source Prefix sub-TLV in the "Babel Sub-TLV Types" registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Because routes can now depend on the sender, a guard rule that only checks the destination might be sneaked around. Rules need updating to look at both.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Set to 128 to indicate a Source Prefix sub-TLV.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the body in octets, excluding the Type and Length fields.

fields.name: Source Plen
fields.desc: Length of the source prefix in bits; MUST NOT be 0.
